sixpence.name: Sixpence
sixpence.description: Tilly, by the fountain in Castle square, has lost her black cat. He has not come in since Sunday. She thinks he is in the churchyard behind the church, where she is not allowed to go.
sixpence.completion: He was on the newest stone, and let himself be carried. Tilly says he is always cold now. She does not seem to mind.

requirements.text: Sixpence, in the churchyard behind the church

sixpence.returnTo: Tilly, by the fountain in Castle square

second_post.name: Second Post
second_post.description: Miss Dray, outside the Post Office on Castle square, has three letters with the wrong numbers on them. They go through three doors in town: the Forge, No. 4 Back Lane, and the Doctor's. Nobody will answer.
second_post.completion: Three letters, three doors, and a mat behind each that sounded thick with others. Miss Dray gave you a key that came to her office with no name on it.

requirements.text: A letter to the Forge, on Cross Lane
A letter to No. 4, Back Lane
A letter to the Doctor's, on Pound Lane

second_post.returnTo: Miss Dray, outside the Post Office on Castle square

washing_day.name: Washing Day
washing_day.description: Mrs Marsh, at her line in front of No. 5 High Street, lost three things to a wind that was not blowing: one by the church door, one by the fountain, and one in the yard of the Castle Arms.
washing_day.completion: A pillowcase, a shirt and a sheet, all bone dry. They went wet. Mrs Marsh gave you two vials of pump water and did not ask where they had been.

requirements.text: Washing, by the church, the fountain and the Arms yard

washing_day.returnTo: Mrs Marsh, at her washing line on the High Street

the_last_name.name: The Last Name
the_last_name.description: Mr Hale, the smith, outside the Forge on Cross Lane, wants the last name on the memorial in Castle square read out to him. His eyes are good. He would rather not be the one who reads it.
the_last_name.completion: HALE, R. He said it back to you the way a man checks a delivery, and gave you two bars of iron from under his bench.

requirements.text: The last name on the memorial, in Castle square

the_last_name.returnTo: the smith, Mr Hale, outside the Forge on Cross Lane

roberts_cap.name: Robert's Cap
roberts_cap.description: Mr Hale says his boy Robert has been up in his room over the Forge since the bell. He wants somebody to knock and tell him his tea is on. He will not go up himself.
roberts_cap.completion: Nobody on the stairs, and his cap on the peg. Mr Hale turned it over in his hands, and gave it back to you to hold.

requirements.text: Robert's cap, on the peg inside the Forge door

roberts_cap.returnTo: the smith, Mr Hale, outside the Forge on Cross Lane

the_new_stone.name: The New Stone
the_new_stone.description: There is a new stone in the churchyard behind the church, with a date on it and no name. Mr Hale wants Robert's cap left on it. He will cut the name himself, when his hands are ready.
the_new_stone.completion: The cap is on the new stone. Mr Hale says he thought the date was for him. He has lit the forge again, and gave you a stone from it that keeps its heat.

requirements.text: The new stone in the churchyard, behind the church

the_new_stone.returnTo: the smith, Mr Hale, outside the Forge on Cross Lane

on_the_hour.name: On the Hour
on_the_hour.description: Mr Dunn, by the telephone box in Castle square, is waiting for his brother to ring. It rang once last week and he could not make it out. He wants somebody younger to lift the receiver and listen.
on_the_hour.completion: A man's voice, a long way off: tell Walter he is at the Arms, and to come before the lamps. Mr Dunn says his brother has never been in a public house in his life.

requirements.text: The telephone box in Castle square

on_the_hour.returnTo: the telephone box in Castle square, and Mr Dunn

the_back_room.name: The Back Room
the_back_room.description: Mr Dunn is chapel and does not go into the Castle Arms. He wants somebody to ask Mrs Garland, who keeps the bar, whether his brother Ernest has been in.
the_back_room.completion: Ernest took the back room in the spring, the night of the bell, and has not come down since. Mr Dunn has stopped waiting by the telephone. He watches the door of the Arms instead.

requirements.text: Mrs Garland, inside the Castle Arms

the_back_room.returnTo: the telephone box in Castle square, and Mr Dunn

the_fourth_lane.name: The Fourth Lane
the_fourth_lane.description: Dot, on Cross Lane, is counting the lanes of Castle. She has three and is sure there used to be four. She wants the name signs read to her. They all stand at the west end of the town, where she is not allowed.
the_fourth_lane.completion: Back Lane, Cross Lane, Pound Lane. Three. Dot gave you a nasturtium she took off Mrs Crewe's stall when nobody was looking.

requirements.text: The Back Lane sign, at the west end of Back Lane
The Cross Lane sign, at the west end of Cross Lane
The Pound Lane sign, at the west end of Pound Lane

school_lane.name: School Lane
school_lane.description: Dot says the lane that runs up past the church to the north gate has no name anywhere in town, and nobody walks up it. There is a sign at the top. Her mum will not take her.
school_lane.completion: CHURCH LANE, and under the paint, SCHOOL LANE. Dot says that is the fourth, and that they do not say it any more. She gave you a key she found in the gutter.

requirements.text: The sign at the top of Church Lane, by the north gate

two_loaves.name: Two Loaves
two_loaves.description: Mrs Oddie, at the bread stall in Castle square, bakes for forty. No. 7 Pound Lane had two loaves every morning, and nobody has been up for them in a fortnight. She wants one left on their step.
two_loaves.completion: The curtain at No. 7 moved to the edge and stopped. Mrs Oddie says they never take it in while there is anyone to see.

requirements.text: A loaf for No. 7, Pound Lane

two_loaves.returnTo: Mrs Oddie, at the bread stall in Castle square

paid_to_sunday.name: Paid to Sunday
paid_to_sunday.description: The Milkman leaves No. 7 its milk every morning and nobody takes it in. He wants the bottles lifted inside the door. There was always money on the mat, he says. He is on his round behind Pound Lane from seven to nine in the morning.
paid_to_sunday.completion: The hall swept, Mrs Oddie's loaf on the table untouched, and the milk money counted out on the mat. The Milkman says it is paid to Sunday. It always is.

requirements.text: The milk on the step of No. 7, Pound Lane

paid_to_sunday.returnTo: the Milkman, on his round behind Pound Lane, seven to nine

never_any_eggs.name: Never Any Eggs
never_any_eggs.description: Mrs Bex comes to the market in Castle square for eggs, and there are never any. She wants somebody to look in the hen house behind Pound Lane, past the green. She would go herself, but she would only find none.
never_any_eggs.completion: Three eggs, and a card with her name on it in her own hand. Mrs Bex does not remember writing it. She gave you grapes, because she had bought too many again.

requirements.text: The hen house behind Pound Lane

never_any_eggs.returnTo: Mrs Bex, at the market in Castle square

white_roses.name: White Roses
white_roses.description: Mr Sallis, in the garden of No. 1 High Street, wants one of his roses taken to his wife Edith. She is in the churchyard behind the church, the first stone inside the gate off the lane. He does not go in.
white_roses.completion: Under the rose you left there were others, dried brown, one for every week. Mr Sallis has not been in since the funeral. He gave you pansies off the bed by his gate.

requirements.text: Edith Sallis's stone, in the churchyard behind the church

white_roses.returnTo: the garden of No. 1, High Street, and Mr Sallis

the_constables_paces.name: A Hundred and Twelve
the_constables_paces.description: The Constable walks the High Street end to end and says it is two paces longer than when he started. He wants somebody else to walk it: from the lamps at the west end to the lamps at the east.
the_constables_paces.completion: You had counted without meaning to: a hundred and fourteen. The Constable wrote it in his book and did not say anything about it.

requirements.text: The lamps at the west end of the High Street
The lamps at the east end of the High Street

the_constables_paces.returnTo: the Constable, walking the High Street

too_red.name: Too Red
too_red.description: Mrs Hobb, in the garden of No. 7 High Street, wants two apples from the orchard behind the house taken to Mr Tolly, on the bench by the memorial in Castle square. He will not pick them. He says they are too red this year.
too_red.completion: Mr Tolly held one up to the light, said it was redder than last year, and ate it anyway.

requirements.text: Two apples, from the orchard behind No. 7, High Street

too_red.returnTo: the bench by the memorial in Castle square, and Mr Tolly
